newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Risk capital fund takes off in Nigeria.
newsitem.headline: Risk capital fund takes off in Nigeria.

text.p: A group of private Nigerian firms on Tuesday launched a fund to provide venture capital to revive and expand ailing businesses in the country.

"The fund is commercial and privately managed, with the principal aim of building up entrepreneurs and their companies," Emmanuel Ocholi, chairman of the National Risk Fund, said at the launching in Lagos.
A three-day workshop of lectures and seminars to explain the working of the fund and capital market began on Tuesday as part of the launch.
"Our mission is to turn ideas and opportunities to viable ventures, return health and growth to ailing businesses," the fund said in a statement.
Shareholders of the fund were blue chip institutions with the financial muscle to take risks and provide funds sourced from the capital market, Ocholi said.
They include six banks, tyre maker Dunlop Industries Nigeria Plc, Cadbury Nigeria Plc, Lever Brothers Nigeria Plc and the government-funded Raw Materials and Development Council of Nigeria.
The fund would target manufacturing companies, which are at the moment the most depressed of the Nigerian economy.
Manufacturers are suffering from low demand for their goods because of the depressed economic situation in the country.
"A low level of capital formation in our economy has impacted adversely the ability to mobilise venture capital for the purpose of risk taking," Ocholi said.
Nigeria's economy, the biggest in Sub-Saharan Africa, has slumped into a recession since the army annulled an election in 1993 meant to restore democracy.

Pragmatic policies in place since the beginning of 1995 have helped stabilise key sectors of the economy but not yet brought significant enough growth to stimulate demand and boost the purchasing power of the population, Africa's largest.
Fred Anigbogu, head of operations of the fund, told Reuters that their method of operation would be by first identifying the problems of a needy company to assess the level of capital to be provided.

"We will then provide capital by buying the shares of the affected company from the capital market. And once we are able to get the business on a sound footing, we divest by selling our shares," he said.
"The amount of risks to be taken by associating with any business will be reduced by our involvement in the daily running of its affairs."
